vignette:
Marcus was 39, a divorced construction worker who had spent most of his adult life doing physically demanding jobs on sites across North America, the kind of work where he was expected to keep moving, keep his head down, and not make a scene. A few years earlier, while working on a roadside renovation, he had witnessed a fatal accident that unfolded in a matter of seconds and then seemed to keep unfolding in his mind long after everyone else had moved on. A crew member had been struck suddenly and violently, and Marcus had seen enough to understand, with immediate horror, that the man was not getting up. What stayed with him was not a full narrative but fragments that arrived as sharply bordered pictures: the angle of the body, the hard glare of daylight on metal, the sudden stillness after impact. When he talked about it, he did so haltingly, as if he were arranging photographs he could never quite bear to look at directly. He also described the sensory details that had lodged in him from that day. At times, when the memory surfaced, he could smell the same hot, dusty odor that had hung in the air at the site, mixed with a faint chemical smell from the machinery, and he would notice the metallic taste that had been in his mouth in the minutes afterward, as though his body had kept a record his mind did not want. 

In the weeks and months that followed, Marcus found that the event no longer stayed in the past in any orderly way. It came back in images, usually without words, intruding when he was driving past an active site, when he caught a whiff of hot asphalt or exhaust near a road crew, or when some taste in his mouth unexpectedly matched the memory enough to make him tense and go quiet. He became deeply convinced that the world no longer worked by any reliable rules. Before, he had believed that if a person did his job, stayed alert, and kept his distance from trouble, things would more or less hold together. Afterward, he had come to believe that belief had been naïve; bad things could happen without warning, and there was nothing he could do to stop them. He spoke of this with a kind of exhausted certainty, saying that the rules he once lived by had been “completely destroyed.” He also felt inadequate in a more personal way, as though witnessing the accident had exposed something weak in him. He knew he had not caused it, but he still judged himself harshly for freezing in the moment and for the fact that, in the aftermath, he could not get his own mind under control. He had become sure that other men on the crew could handle things better than he could, and that he had somehow failed the basic test of being capable and steady.

Over time, Marcus began shaping his days around not having to feel what came up. He made a point of never allowing himself to feel or show anger, even when it seemed to rise in him unexpectedly. He described anger as dangerous and useless, something that might take him somewhere he could not manage, so he held it down with nearly military discipline. At other times he tried to blank out entirely, deliberately leaving himself in a kind of mental fog until the moment passed. He also started gambling, first in small amounts and then more regularly, saying that the pull of it was the brief distraction and the excitement, the sharp focus on something other than his own head. These habits fit around the rest of his life in ways that were costly but gradual enough that he adjusted to them before fully noticing what they were costing him. He was more detached with people, including his former wife before the divorce, and there were times when she complained that he seemed absent even when he was sitting right next to her. At work, he could still function, but he was more likely to keep to himself and to feel rattled when the site environment brought the memory close again, especially around heavy equipment, loud impact noises, or the kind of hot, dusty air that made the accident feel suddenly present.

By the time he sought help, Marcus was no longer able to dismiss the problem as something he should simply tough out. The symptoms had accumulated into a level of distress that was beginning to interfere more openly with his work, his relationships, and his sense of himself. He came in with the guarded expression of a man who was used to handling things alone, but there was also a sense that he was tired of being ruled by images, smells, and tastes he had never chosen to keep. What finally brought him to treatment was the growing fear that he could not keep suppressing everything forever, and that if he did not find some way to face what had happened, he would remain stuck in the conviction that the world was broken, that disaster was unavoidable, and that he was fundamentally not enough to meet it.
